findings.headline: Mid Devon's share of the pan-Devon claim for paused Local Government Reorganisation costs is c£207k
findings.detail: Following the government's pause of Local Government Reorganisation, a pan-Devon claim has been submitted to recover costs incurred to date. Mid Devon's share includes both direct and estimated indirect costs.
findings.matters: A reorganisation cost recovery claim with a specific share is a one-off cost other councils involved in reorganisation will be tracking.
findings.figures: c£207k Mid Devon share of claim
findings.quote: Following the Government announcement to pause Local Government Reorganisation

findings.headline: Two of four remaining Hadden Heights units to be rented for a period, with two kept available to buy
findings.detail: The paper says interest in Hadden Heights remains subdued, with one sale progressing and few viewings. Renting two units is intended to reduce the cost of holding the premises. The strategy can be reviewed if the market picks up.
findings.matters: A council switching from selling to renting part of a development to reduce holding costs is a decision other councils with unsold stock will compare.
findings.figures: two of four remaining units rented
findings.quote: renting two of the four remaining units (one of each style) for a period, leaving the other two available to buy.

findings.headline: Procurement Regulations changed on 1 April 2026, requiring a contract or waiver before any purchase order
findings.detail: The paper says the change has increased the number of waivers in the short term, but this should reduce as they progress into formal contracts. It describes the change as improving compliance.
findings.matters: A rule change requiring a contract or waiver before any purchase order is applied will affect how other councils manage procurement compliance from April 2026.
findings.figures: Procurement Regulations changed 1 April 2026
findings.quote: It should be noted that the Procurement Regulations changed on the 1 April 2026, which now requires a contract or waiver to be in place before any purchase order can be placed.

findings.headline: 564 social rent refunds totalling £348,022.60 issued to tenants, with the DWP still to clarify its approach
findings.detail: The paper reports 564 refunds issued to tenants following social rent error correction, including £14,625 in compensation. Officers are still chasing the DWP for a plan to settle the issue, and the regulator is engaged.
findings.matters: A housing rent correction involving refunds, compensation and regulator engagement is a governance matter other housing landlords and councils will recognise.
findings.figures: 564 refunds; £348,022.60 total value; £14,625 compensation
findings.quote: To date, 564 refunds have been issued to tenants, with a total value of £348,022.60

findings.headline: Council tax collection rate slightly below the 97.5% target
findings.detail: Collection rate data indicates the council is slightly below its 97.5% target. The year-end position is difficult to forecast, and any variance will be accounted for in the following year.
findings.matters: A council tax collection rate below target affects the taxbase and Collection Fund position that other councils and lenders track.
findings.figures: 97.5% collection target
findings.quote: collection rate data indicates that we are slightly below the 97.5% target.

findings.headline: Business rates forecast potential gain of c£600k, subject to a government baseline reset
findings.detail: The forecast gain comes from the council's taxbase being higher than the government's assumption in the finance settlement. The government has announced a further baseline reset that could reduce or remove the gain, and the impact has not yet been assessed.
findings.matters: A business rates gain dependent on a baseline reset is one other councils will be watching as the reset is confirmed.
findings.figures: c£600k potential business rates gain
findings.quote: However, the Government have announced a further reset of the baseline which could reduce or remove this potential gain.

findings.headline: Council funding capital from reserves rather than borrowing, with £220k lower treasury income and £100k less interest payable
findings.detail: The paper says the HRA's treasury income is £220k lower because cash balances are being used to fund the delivery programme from reserves instead of borrowing. Maximising internal borrowing reduces interest payable by £100k and delays the need for external borrowing.
findings.matters: Using reserves instead of external borrowing is a funding choice that other councils and lenders will see as a change in the council's external borrowing timing.
findings.figures: £220k treasury income reduction; £100k less interest payable
findings.quote: as a direct consequence of funding the delivery programme via reserves as opposed to borrowing.

findings.headline: HRA forecast £28k net underspend after £1,016k PWLB smoothing reserve contribution is redirected to the HRA reserve
findings.detail: The £1,016k budgeted contribution to the PWLB Smoothing Reserve is no longer needed following the policy change from 2025/26 outturn, so it is recommended to replenish the HRA reserve instead. The HRA reserve is forecast to rise from £455k to £1,499k.
findings.matters: A policy change that removes a planned reserve contribution and moves the funds to the HRA reserve is a reserve movement other finance directors will want to compare.
findings.figures: £28k net underspend; £1,016k PWLB smoothing reserve contribution; HRA reserve £455k at 31/03/2026, £1,499k forecast at 31/03/2027
findings.quote: This shows a good improvement in the position of the HRA following the work undertaken to address the additional burdens faced by the service.

findings.headline: HRA housing development slippage of £14,687k from procurement, legal, planning and decant delays
findings.detail: The paper attributes HRA slippage to procurement, legal and planning delays, and to decants from current properties. Several projects are awaiting viability assessments. The new HRA depot's planning and tender are expected to complete in 2026/27.
findings.matters: HRA development slippage of this scale affects a council's housing delivery and its borrowing profile, which matters to lenders.
findings.figures: £14,687k HRA slippage; £916k overspends; £1,304k underspends
findings.quote: There are a few delays on the HRA housing developments

findings.headline: Cullompton Town Centre Relief Road starting later than planned, with £5,390k General Fund slippage
findings.detail: The paper says the General Fund slippage is largely from the Cullompton Town Centre Relief Road. Delays came from the Compulsory Purchase Order and the relocation of the Bowls Club and Football Club. Construction has now started, and solar project tendering is also delayed.
findings.matters: A flagship road scheme delayed by land acquisition and relocation is the kind of project delay other councils and their lenders track.
findings.figures: £5,390k General Fund slippage
findings.quote: due to starting on site later than planned following delays with the Compulsory Purchase Order

findings.headline: Capital spend forecast at £31,729k for 2026/27, with £20,076k slipping into future years
findings.detail: Actual and forecast capital spend is £31,729k against the revised deliverable programme of £52,061k. Of the £20,332k variance, £1,654k is underspend, £1,518k is overspend, and £120k is no longer required.
findings.matters: A slippage rate of this size against a deliverable programme is a delivery risk that other councils and lenders will want to track.
findings.figures: £31,729k actual and forecast spend; £52,061k deliverable budget; £20,332k variance; £20,076k slippage; £1,654k underspend; £1,518k overspend; £120k no longer required
findings.quote: Of which, £1,654k is an under spend, £1,518k is an overspend and £20,076k will slip into future years.

findings.headline: Cabinet asked to pursue reserve review, vacancy freezes and fee increases to reduce the shortfall
findings.detail: Recommendation 1b asks the S151 Officer to review reserves and possible one-off mitigations, implement vacancy freezes where appropriate, and review fees and charges. The paper suggests raising fees ahead of the normal April timeframe.
findings.matters: The mix of reserve draw, recruitment freeze and early fee increases is the same toolkit other councils use when a General Fund overspend is forecast.
findings.figures: Recommendation 1b, three actions to address the shortfall shown in paragraph 3.8
findings.quote: A freeze in recruitment could be implemented.

findings.headline: Fuel costs adding over £150k of pressure to service costs
findings.detail: The paper says escalating fuel costs are adding to service costs and are largely beyond the council's control without changing service provision. Electrifying part of the vehicle fleet has reduced the impact.
findings.matters: Fuel-driven pressure on waste and fleet budgets is a cost that other councils running their own vehicle fleets are likely to face.
findings.figures: over £150k added fuel pressure
findings.quote: Escalating fuel costs are also affecting service costs, with over £150k of added pressure being felt.

findings.headline: Agency staff costs offset £229k of the £436k forecast employee underspend
findings.detail: Employee costs are forecast £436k under budget after the £282k vacancy target. Agency cover for long-term vacancies, mainly in Waste, more than offsets the service underspends by £229k. The council says it is recruiting apprentices and reviewing all vacancies.
findings.matters: A council using agency staff to cover vacancies in front-line services, with the cost exceeding the salary saving, is a pattern other finance officers will compare against their own vacancy targets.
findings.figures: £436k forecast employee underspend; £282k vacancy target; £229k agency cost offset
findings.quote: The cost of the agency staff more than offsets the corresponding General Fund service

findings.headline: Full-year forecast income variance of £195k below budget, mainly planning income
findings.detail: The paper attributes the shortfall mainly to lower planning income, linked to the housing market and higher borrowing costs, plus delays to major schemes. Waste income is also behind expectations, while leisure and the Pannier Market are also projecting shortfalls.
findings.matters: Planning and waste fee income shortfalls, alongside a government fee rise, are pressures other councils dependent on fee-earning services will recognise.
findings.figures: £195k full-year income shortfall against budget
findings.quote: It shows that the full year forecast Income variance is £195k below budget, mainly due to lower than expecting planning income

findings.headline: General Fund reserve forecast to fall from £2,091k to £1,135k, below the agreed minimum £2m balance
findings.detail: The paper says the forecast overspend would reduce the General Reserve to £1,135k, below the agreed minimum of £2m. It says the position will be reviewed at year end alongside the significant loss of central government core funding. Earmarked reserves are forecast to move from £17,327k to £17,075k.
findings.matters: A General Fund reserve below its own minimum, with a year-end review pending, is a position other finance directors and lenders will want to track.
findings.figures: General Fund reserve £2,091k at 31/03/2026, £1,135k forecast at 31/03/2027, agreed minimum £2m; GF earmarked reserves £17,327k to £17,075k
findings.quote: If the forecast level of overspend is delivered, this will indicatively decrease the General Reserve balance to £1,135k, below the agreed minimum £2m balance.

findings.headline: General Fund forecast overspend of £956k after transfers to and from earmarked reserves
findings.detail: The forecast General Fund overspend is £956k after EMR transfers, against a total net cost of services budget of £15,384,260. Officers have identified some unbudgeted spend that can be mitigated from earmarked reserves, and Appendix A shows the service-level detail.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare how an authority is funding a £956k in-year General Fund overspend, including the use of earmarked reserves to offset it.
findings.figures: £956k overspend after EMRs; Total Net Cost of Services £15,384,260 budget, £16,276,610 forecast, £892,350 variance
findings.quote: The forecast General Fund overspend for the current year is £956k after transfers to and from earmarked reserves.

findings.detail: The appendix records direct award MD26123 for £250,000.00, dated 10/08/2026, described as 'Section 106 contributions following developments'. The framework column is recorded as 'n/a'.
findings.matters: Section 106 funds paid out by direct award without a framework are a route finance officers would want to see tied to the agreements that generated the contributions.

findings.detail: Direct award MD26129 renews the Idox licence and support, with a value of £404,439.00 inc. VAT and a start date of 31/10/2026. It is placed through the CCS framework.
findings.matters: A licence renewal of this size is a recurring cost a finance director would track against the ICT budget, and the framework route is a point of comparison for peers renewing the same system.
findings.quote: MD26129 £404,439.00 Idox licence and support renewal 31/10/2026 CCS

findings.detail: Direct award MD26073 is for NEC Workflow, with a value of £601,200.00 inc. VAT and a start date of 01/08/2026. It is placed through the CCS framework and is the largest direct award in the appendix.
findings.matters: A software contract of this value placed as a direct award through a framework is one a finance director would check against the procurement route and the software budget.
findings.quote: MD26073 £601,200.00 NEC Workflow

findings.paper_title: Appendix G - Procurement Waivers and Direct Awards Qtr 2
findings.headline: Waiver WV26068 for £180,000.00 covers provision of internal audit services, dated 21/09/2026.
findings.detail: The appendix records waiver WV26068 for £180,000.00, dated 21/09/2026, for internal audit services. It is the largest single waiver in the Quarter 2 list.
findings.matters: An internal audit contract of this size placed by waiver rather than tender is one an audit committee and finance teams at other councils would compare against their own internal audit procurement.
findings.quote: WV26068 21/09/2026 £180,000.00 Provision of internal audit services

findings.paper_title: Appendix G - Procurement Waivers and Direct Awards Qtr 2
findings.headline: Waiver WV26046 for £200,000.00 covers provision of temporary accommodation, dated 01/07/2026.
findings.detail: The appendix records waiver WV26046 for £200,000.00, dated 01/07/2026, described as 'Provision of temporary accommodation'. No further detail on the service or period is given in this appendix.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation spend procured by waiver rather than competitive tender is a housing cost a finance director would want to track against budget.
findings.quote: WV26046 01/07/2026 £200,000.00 Provision of temporary accommodation

findings.headline: Statutory planning fees and charges in Q2 are £150,000 below the prior year.
findings.detail: The paper reports that Q2 statutory planning fee and charge performance is down on the prior year by £150,000, within the Planning service variance.
findings.matters: Falling planning fee income in a service that is also carrying agency and local plan costs compounds the pressure, which other councils with similar planning services will recognise.
findings.figures: £150,000 shortfall in statutory planning fees and charges against prior year
findings.quote: Q2 performance of statutory planning fees and charges down on prior year 150,000

findings.headline: Investment income is forecast £60,000 lower due to reduced cash balances.
findings.detail: Interest receivable is forecast to fall by £60,000 because the council holds lower cash balances. The paper attributes the change to cash balances, not to interest rates.
findings.matters: Falling cash balances reduce investment income and may signal drawdown of reserves or cash used to fund capital spending, which is relevant to lenders and treasury teams.
findings.figures: £60,000 reduction in investment income
findings.quote: Investment income down due to reduced cash balances 60,000

findings.headline: Planned maintenance in Property Services is £270,000 under budget, with schedules still being scoped and work not yet started.
findings.detail: The underspend reflects planned maintenance schedules that are being scoped and will be tendered. The paper states that the work has yet to start, so the saving is a timing difference rather than a confirmed reduction in spend.
findings.matters: A large underspend on planned maintenance that has not yet been tendered indicates a deferred liability that will affect future years.
findings.figures: (£270,000) planned maintenance underspend
findings.quote: Planned Maintenance schedules being scoped and will be tendered - work has yet to be started (270,000)

findings.headline: Waste Services shows £375,000 of additional agency cost from vacancies, sickness and increased household collections, alongside £138,350 of higher fuel costs.
findings.detail: The Waste Services lines include agency cover of £375,000 linked to vacancies, sickness and collection volumes, and fuel costs £138,350 higher than budget. Vehicle maintenance outside the contract and lower recycling credits and income also appear in the same service.
findings.matters: Staffing cover and fuel costs in frontline collection services are common budget pressures, and the paper ties this one to specific causes that other councils can compare against their own.
findings.figures: £375,000 agency cost; £138,350 fuel costs; £100,000 reduction in recycling credits; £70,000 vehicle maintenance outside contract
findings.quote: Increased agency due to vacancies, sickness and increased household collections 375,000

findings.headline: The local plan is forecast £288,900 over budget, with £180,900 funded from earmarked reserves and £108,000 of capacity funding received.
findings.detail: Planning shows an overspend on the local plan of £288,900. The paper records £180,900 of this being met from earmarked reserves, and separately records £108,000 of capacity funding received for the local plan.
findings.matters: Plan-making costs funded from reserves and one-off capacity grant are a pressure several councils face, and the split shows how much relies on non-recurring funding.
findings.figures: £288,900 overspend on local plan; (£180,900) funded by EMR; (£108,000) capacity funding received
findings.quote: Overspend on local plan funded by EMR and capacity funding 288,900 (180,900)

findings.headline: Revenue Support Grant fell by £426,799 in the Final Settlement, and a one-off grant of £426,799 has been set against the reduction.
findings.detail: The Final Settlement reduced Revenue Support Grant by £426,799. The paper offsets this movement with a one-off grant of the same amount, so the net effect on the General Fund variance is nil.
findings.matters: Finance officers elsewhere will want to know how a settlement reduction is being met in a year where the offset is one-off rather than recurring.
findings.figures: £426,799 reduction in Revenue Support Grant; £426,799 one-off grant offset
findings.quote: One-off grant to cover movement in RSG announced in Final Settlement (426,799)

findings.headline: Mid Devon's total forecast General Fund deficit at 31/03/2027 is £956,488, after a £236,454 transfer from earmarked reserves.
findings.detail: The paper shows a service forecast deficit of £1,178,804 and a non-service forecast surplus of £222,316. Earmarked reserve movements of (£236,454) reduce the total deficit to £956,488 at 31/03/2027.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare how much of a forecast in-year gap is being met from earmarked reserves rather than from new savings or income.
findings.figures: £956,488 total forecast deficit; £1,178,804 service forecast deficit; (£222,316) non-service forecast surplus; (£236,454) net transfer from earmarked reserves
findings.quote: Total Forecast (Surplus)/Deficit as at 31/03/2027 956,488 (236,454)

findings.headline: Financial Services agency costs are £67,564 at period 6 with nothing profiled, and a full-year forecast variation of £67,500.
findings.detail: The finance function shows agency staff costs of £67,564 at period 6, with a profiled budget of nil. The full-year forecast variation is £67,500 against an annual agency budget of nil. Revenues & Benefits shows agency costs of £50,513 at P6 with a full-year forecast variation of £70,000.
findings.matters: A finance director can compare how much agency cover the finance and revenues functions are carrying, which matters for the resilience of the same service at other councils.
findings.figures: Financial Services: annual agency budget £0; P6 profiled £0; P6 actual £67,564; P6 variance £67,564; full-year forecast variation £67,500. Revenues & Benefits: P6 actual £50,513; full-year forecast variation £70,000
findings.quote: Financial Services 0 0 67,564 67,564 67,500 0.0%

findings.detail: Corporate Management's P6 actual employee costs are £718,956 against £619,654 profiled, a variance of £99,302. The full-year forecast variation is £167,000. Property Services shows a P6 variance of (£74,146) and a full-year forecast variation of (£166,000) on an annual budget of £806,100.
findings.matters: A finance director can see that two service lines are forecast to move in opposite directions by similar amounts, which is the kind of offset a council reports against its overall staffing budget.
findings.figures: Corporate Management: annual budget £1,239,310; P6 profiled £619,654; P6 actual £718,956; P6 variance £99,302 (13.5%); full-year forecast variation £167,000. Property Services: annual budget £806,100; P6 profiled £403,050; P6 actual £328,904; P6 variance (£74,146) (-20.6%); full-year forecast variation (£166,000)

findings.detail: Waste Services is the largest agency line in the General Fund table. Its P6 agency variance is £182,646, and the full-year forecast variation is £375,000 against an annual agency budget of £42,860. The same service's employee costs show a full-year forecast variation of (£180,000).
findings.matters: A finance director at another council running a similar waste service can see how much of the agency cover is building against the employee underspend in the same service.
findings.figures: Annual agency budget £42,860; P6 profiled £21,430; P6 actual £204,076; P6 variance £182,646; full-year forecast variation £375,000; variance 874.9%; employee full-year forecast variation (£180,000)

findings.headline: Total employee costs are £11,333,052 at period 6 against a profiled £11,625,244, with a full-year forecast variation of (£436,000).
findings.detail: Across the General Fund and HRA, employee costs are £292,192 below the profiled budget at period 6. The full-year forecast variation is shown as (£436,000) against an annual budget of £23,283,080. The paper's table records the variance as a negative figure.
findings.matters: A finance director can compare the employee cost underspend with the agency overspend in the same table to see whether vacancy savings are offsetting agency cover.
findings.figures: Annual budget £23,283,080; P6 profiled £11,625,244; P6 actual £11,333,052; P6 variance (£292,192); full-year forecast variation (£436,000); variance -1.9%

findings.detail: The General Fund agency line totals £524,977 actual against £32,010 profiled, a variance of £492,967. The full-year forecast variation is £665,000 on an annual agency budget of £64,020. Agency spend appears in most of the service rows in the second table.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare how quickly agency spend is building against its profiled budget, and a lender can see how much of the staffing cost sits outside the establishment.
findings.figures: Annual agency budget £64,020; P6 profiled £32,010; P6 actual £524,977; P6 variance £492,967; full-year forecast variation £665,000; variance 1038.7%

findings.detail: Licensing has an annual budget of £175,880. The period 6 actual is £40,185 above the profiled figure, the largest favourable variance in the table in money terms, and the full-year forecast variation is shown as 0.
findings.matters: Licensing income running ahead of profile at the half-year point is a result a finance director at another council may want to examine for its own licensing budgets.
findings.figures: Annual budget £175,880; profiled budget £76,241; actual £116,427; variance £40,185; full-year forecast variation £0

findings.matters: A period 6 shortfall alongside a nil full-year forecast variation shows the council expects to recover the gap by year end, a position a finance director would want to test against car parking demand elsewhere.
findings.figures: Annual budget £1,078,420; profiled budget £523,944; actual £493,400; variance £30,545; full-year forecast variation £0

findings.matters: A forecast variation of more than a fifth of a small income stream is a sign that a council's market income assumptions may not hold, which other councils with market operations would want to check against their own budgets.

findings.matters: The aggregate forecast variation shows how much the council expects its fees and charges base to move by year end, which is the figure a peer council would compare its own income monitoring against.

findings.detail: The paper says Bank Rate is expected to increase in the near term because of energy-driven inflation, then ease over the next year or two. The forecast is based on PWLB certainty rates, which the advisers set at gilt yields plus 80bps.
findings.matters: These forecasts set the rate at which the new borrowing of up to £8.000m would be taken, so a finance officer at another council with similar borrowing plans would read them as the market expectation for their own refinancing.

findings.detail: The Council's share of the £5m CCLA fund is now valued at £4.468m. Dividends for the first two quarters were £106k at 4.26%, up from £103k at 4.10% a year earlier.
findings.matters: A fall in the capital value of a property fund holding alongside rising dividends shows a split between income and capital that a peer council holding the same kind of investment would want to compare.

findings.quote: There has been a decrease in fund value of £75k during the first half of 2026/27

findings.detail: The paper reports no short-term borrowing. Forecast year-end debt is £37.607m, against an original estimate of £39,663k, with other long-term liabilities falling from £7,189k to £4,333k.
findings.matters: PWLB exposure and forecast year-end debt are the core figures a lender uses to assess a council's borrowing position, and this paper gives both for the half year.

findings.headline: The revised capital financing requirement for 2026/27 is £68,565k, down from an original £83,187k, after the capital programme was revised to a deliverable level
findings.detail: The paper says the treasury strategy must be revised because the capital programme has been reset to one that is deliverable. The housing CFR falls from £67,627k to £51,252k, while the non-housing CFR rises from £15,560k to £17,313k. The authorised limit falls from £93,000k to £78,000k.
findings.matters: A council cutting its CFR and authorised limit by about £15m after a reset of the capital programme shows how much borrowing headroom has changed, which affects how lenders assess its future debt.
findings.figures: CFR £83,187k original, £68,565k revised; housing CFR £67,627k original, £51,252k revised; non-housing CFR £15,560k original, £17,313k revised; authorised limit £93,000k original, £78,000k revised; operational boundary £84,000k original, £69,000k revised
findings.quote: requires revision in light of a revised deliverable Capital Programme

findings.headline: The paper says new borrowing of up to £8.000m is likely before the end of 2026/27, up from an original forecast of £7.200m
findings.detail: No new borrowing has been taken so far this year. The paper attributes the increase to capital overspends being funded by borrowing and reserves.
findings.matters: A council increasing its planned borrowing because of capital overspends is a signal a lender and a peer finance officer will want to track, especially with PWLB rates forecast to remain high.
findings.figures: up to £8.000m new borrowing forecast; £7.200m original forecast; no new borrowing taken to date in 2026/27
findings.quote: it is likely that new borrowing of up to £8.000m will be required before the end of the financial year

findings.headline: Short-term investments stood at £5.28m at 30 September 2026, against £8.000m at the same point last year
findings.detail: The paper links the fall to increased use of internal balances to fund the capital programme. It also says cash balances will fall further towards year end, so investment income is expected to stay at a similar level in the second half.
findings.matters: Using internal balances to fund capital reduces the cash available for investment, which is the same mechanism a peer council would see when it runs down reserves to pay for capital.
findings.figures: £5.28m short-term investments and deposits at 30/09/2026; £8.000m at the same point in 2025/26; £3.00m in fixed term investments; £2.28m in NatWest call accounts; £5.00m in CCLA fund
findings.quote: mainly due to increased use of internal balances to support the capital programme, leaving less for investment.

findings.headline: Investment income to 30/09/2026 is £230k against a forecast year-end of £443k, and the paper says performance is below budget expectations
findings.detail: The paper gives the average return on investments as 3.71% for the first six months, down from 4.51% a year earlier. It attributes the shortfall to lower cash balances available for investment.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare this forecast against their own investment budget, and a lender can see that treasury income is falling below plan as cash balances decline.
findings.figures: £230k total interest to 30/09/2026; £443k forecast year-end total; £192k General Fund and £38k HRA to date; General Fund investment budget £430k; HRA investment budget £288k; average return 3.71% (previous year 4.51%)

findings.matters: A General Fund programme forecasting roughly a fifth less spend than its adjusted 2026/27 plan, mainly through slippage, is a pattern finance officers at other councils will be comparing with their own Q2 positions.

findings.headline: Financing of capital expenditure is forecast £120,000 (9%) below budget, and the paper cites capital programme slippage as a reason for a reduction in MRP.
findings.detail: The paper says the MRP reduction is due to capital programme slippage and using reserves to fund capital in favour of borrowing. The financing of capital expenditure line is forecast at £1,170,200 against a £1,290,200 budget.
findings.matters: Capital slippage reduces the MRP charge in the short term, but a council that funds capital from reserves rather than borrowing is changing its debt profile, which a lender or peer finance team would want to track.

findings.detail: The paper gives the reason as investment income being down due to lower cash balances. This is the largest adverse movement on the HRA income side and sits alongside the reduction in interest payable.
findings.matters: A finance director would want to see the income cost of internal borrowing set against the interest saving, to judge whether the trade-off is worth it.
findings.figures: Budget £288,000; forecast £68,000; variance £220,000 (76%)
findings.quote: Investment income down due to lower cash balances

findings.detail: The paper attributes the reduction to maximisation of internal borrowing, which limits the need for external borrowing. The same section records that investment income is lower because of lower cash balances, so the two movements are linked.
findings.matters: A council choosing internal borrowing over external borrowing changes both its interest bill and its interest income, and here the paper shows both moving in the same direction.
findings.figures: Budget £912,000; forecast £812,000; variance (100,000) (-11%)
findings.quote: Reduction in interest payable due to maximisation of internal

findings.matters: This is the single largest favourable variance in the HRA, and it is the reason the forecast surplus is so large; a finance director would want to know it comes from dropping a planned reserve contribution, not from operating performance.
findings.quote: Contribution to PWLB Smoothing reserve no longer required

findings.detail: The HRA is budgeted to break even for 2026/27, but the period 6 actual shows a surplus of (2,797,485) and the full-year forecast is a surplus of (1,044,400). The paper shows the reserve balance moving from (455,000) at 31/03/2026 to a forecast (1,499,400) at 31/03/2027.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare how a forecast in-year HRA surplus of this size is being used to rebuild the HRA reserve, against the budgeted nil position.

findings.quote: Forecast HRA Reserve Balance 31/03/2027 (1,499,400)

findings.matters: Lower interest receivable on cash balances is a direct consequence of the council holding less cash, a position a lender or peer finance officer would want to track alongside reserve drawdowns.

findings.matters: A revenues and benefits overspend of this proportion, with no reserve cover, bears directly on the cost of collecting council tax and business rates that funds the council.

findings.matters: A service-level overspend of more than a third of its budget, with no reserve offset, is the kind of pressure a finance director at a peer council would want to benchmark against their own waste contract costs.

findings.matters: Weak debt collection directly affects the council's cash flow and may be an early warning sign of deteriorating financial position among the council's debtors, a leading indicator of broader economic stress in the district.

findings.matters: Planning fee income volatility indicates changes in local development activity or fee-earning planning work. This affects the council's discretionary resources and is a leading indicator of economic activity in the district.

findings.headline: Service revenue budgets across three major portfolios are projected to overspend by approximately £700k in Q1.
findings.detail: Planning Environment & Sustainability is £180k over, Homes General Fund £50k over, and Service Delivery £475k over. These are not isolated pressures. The pattern of simultaneous overspends across different service areas suggests cost pressures may be structural rather than one-off, raising questions about whether the base budget is sufficient or whether inflationary pressures are outpacing provision.
findings.matters: Multiple simultaneous revenue overspends across different service portfolios indicate systemic cost pressures that may persist and constrain the council's financial flexibility and reserves drawdown.
findings.figures: PE&S overspend £180k (£1,414k vs £1,234k); Homes overspend £50k (£748k vs £698k); SD&CI overspend £475k (£5,046k vs £4,571k)

findings.headline: Capital project implementation is delayed across all council service areas, with Planning Environment & Sustainability at 75% slippage and HRA capital £12m underspent.
findings.detail: Systematic delays in capital project delivery span multiple portfolios: PE&S at 75%, HRA 47%, Economy & Assets 41%, and Service Delivery 24%. The HRA alone shows £12m underspent on a £25.5m budget. This pattern raises questions about whether the council has realistic project timelines, adequate delivery capacity, or whether external constraints are blocking progress.
findings.matters: Persistent capital slippage across multiple portfolios is a primary indicator of execution risk for a lender considering borrowing facilities. It signals either that capital programmes are mispriced or the council lacks capacity to deploy borrowed funds effectively.
findings.figures: PE&S capital slippage 75% (£70k spent vs £960k budget); HRA capital slippage 47% (£13,510k vs £25,555k); E&A slippage 41%; SD&CI slippage 24%
findings.quote: PE&S PDG – Projected Capital Outturn £70k £960k R

findings.headline: Housing and Regeneration Development delivered only 7 new social housing units against an annual target of 100 in Q1 2026/27.
findings.detail: Mid Devon Housing is significantly behind on social housing delivery. In parallel, 16 households are in hotels and £84,615 was spent on interim accommodation in a single quarter. HRA capital projects are 47% behind schedule, with only £13.5m of a £25.5m capital budget projected to be spent. This suggests both capacity and planning constraints are impeding housing delivery during an acknowledged housing crisis.
findings.matters: Severe underperformance in housing delivery at this scale indicates deep execution constraints or strategic misalignment that will require material remedial action, and reflects on the council's broader delivery capacity.
findings.figures: 7 new homes delivered (target: 100); 16 households in hotels; £84,615 spent on interim accommodation April-June; HRA capital £13,510k vs £25,555k budget; 47% of HRA development projects behind
findings.quote: MDH Delivery of new Social Housing (YTD) 7 100 R

findings.headline: Commercial property vacancy rate at 10%, above the 5% target
findings.detail: The council's commercial and retail property portfolio comprises 60 leases across Tiverton, Cullompton, and Phoenix House. At the end of Q1 2026/27, 6 leases (10%) were vacant, performing below the 5% vacancy target. No explanation is provided for the higher vacancy rate.
findings.matters: Commercial property income is asset-backed revenue; higher vacancy rates reduce rental income and may signal softening local business demand or economic conditions that could affect the council's income base.
findings.figures: 10% vacancy rate (6 of 60 leases); 5% target
findings.quote: 10% of the available 60 commercial leases were vacant at the end of Quarter 1 2026/27, performing behind target (5%).

findings.headline: Housing programme delivered 7 homes in Q1 2026/27 against annual target of 100, significantly behind plan
findings.detail: Mid Devon Housing added seven homes to its stock in Q1 2026/27, all built to net zero standards. This represents 7% of the annual 100-home target achieved in the first quarter. The council notes these indicators are expected to remain below target during the year, with delivery weighted towards later quarters as capital schemes complete.
findings.matters: Capital investment programmes and their delivery profiles affect a council's borrowing needs and financial forecasts; early-quarter underperformance, even if framed as expected timing, can indicate delivery risks or assumptions worth monitoring.
findings.figures: 7 homes delivered; 100 homes target for 2026/27
findings.quote: Seven homes have become part of Mid Devon Housing in 2026/27 so far. Performance is behind target (100 homes for 2026/27).

findings.headline: Leisure service cost per visit more than doubled to £1.52 from £0.84, driven by national insurance contributions and pay award pressures
findings.detail: The cost per visit to leisure services in 2025/26 increased 82% compared to 2024/25, from £0.84 to £1.52. The council attributes this to national insurance contribution pressures, the local government pay award, and significant investment in new changing facilities at both swimming pools. The paper explicitly notes there was a larger deficit between income and costs in 2025/26.
findings.matters: Cost pressures from NI contributions and pay awards are external factors beyond council control; where these create service deficits, they signal budget strain and potential impacts on other services, borrowing needs, or reserves.
findings.quote: There was a larger deficit between income and costs in 2025/26, largely due to national insurance contribution pressures, the local government pay award and significant investment in new changing facilities at both swimming pools.

findings.headline: Housing delivery programme advancing with 75 new homes in 2025/26 and Local Authority Housing Fund award for 4 additional temporary accommodation properties
findings.detail: Council delivering housing through multiple routes: 75 new additions to stock planned for 2025/26 with additional schemes in HRA development programme pipeline; Local Authority Housing Fund Round 4 bid awarded for 4 additional temporary accommodation properties; former vets property conversion for temporary accommodation in Tiverton completed tender and commenced site works May 2026.
findings.matters: Housing delivery affects council's ability to manage homelessness costs and impacts strategic regeneration objectives. Lenders track housing delivery as evidence of strategic execution and demand management capability.
findings.figures: 75 new additions to stock 2025/26; 4 additional TA properties funded; former vets conversion site works commenced May 2026
findings.quote: Bid awarded from Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government for latest Local Authority Housing Fund (Round 4) funding to further support TA provision - 4no. additional properties supported. ... Former vets property for conversion to additional Temporary Accommodation (TA) in Tiverton tender for conversion completed and contract awarded, site works commenced May 2026.

findings.headline: Culm Garden Village project has no assurance of capacity funding for next financial year despite securing current year funding
findings.detail: Capacity funding required for project team and leadership function has been secured for the current financial year 2025/26. No assurances exist for the following year. Officers are proactively engaging with Homes England seeking further funding rounds and identifying alternative opportunities from landowners and developers involved in the project.
findings.matters: Funding uncertainty for delivery projects creates programme delivery risk and can affect planned housing and regeneration outcomes. Lenders care about whether major development programmes can sustain as planned.
findings.figures: One financial year of funding secured
findings.quote: Capacity funding was secured for the last financial year; however, we do not currently have any assurances of funding for the next financial year.

findings.headline: Cullompton Town Centre Relief Road progressing with compulsory purchase order confirmation expected by end of May and main works commencing July
findings.detail: Major infrastructure project tracking to schedule with funding secured from Homes England. Land assembly near completion. Advanced enabling works have been undertaken in readiness for main road works to commence in July 2026. Project has healthy risk allowance with risks being mitigated as works progress.
findings.matters: Material capital project delivery on schedule indicates council capability in executing major infrastructure programmes. Lenders track capex delivery as evidence of project management and execution risk control.
findings.figures: Homes England funding secured; CPO confirmation expected end of May; main works July 2026
findings.quote: Works are progressing well on the delivery of the relief road. The majority of land required is near to being secured with confirmation of the Compulsory Purchase Order expected by the end of May. Advanced enabling works have been undertaken in readiness for the main road works commencing in July.

findings.headline: Regulator for Social Housing published satisfaction with council's actions on historic housing rent error correction
findings.detail: The council's correction process for a previously identified housing rent error has been formally assessed by the Regulator for Social Housing and found acceptable. Regular monitoring arrangements remain in place. Most current tenancy cases have been resolved and refunds are commencing on former cases, though some cases dependent on DWP action remain pending.
findings.matters: Regulatory satisfaction represents material de-risking of a significant compliance and reputational issue. Lenders care about resolution of regulatory findings and management of housing finance risks.
findings.figures: Most current (live) tenancy cases resolved; progress with former cases and refunds commenced; ongoing cases awaiting DWP action
findings.quote: Regulatory decision published by Regulator of Social Housing (RSH) who are satisfied with actions taken to address historic error. Regular monitoring arrangements in place between RSH and Council on plan implementation.

findings.headline: Government local government reorganisation decision expected June/July 2026 with all 11 Devon councils collaborating on asset and resource databases for transition planning
findings.detail: The council and 10 peer authorities are preparing for major structural reorganisation under Government devolution plans creating strategic authorities of 1.5m population headed by elected mayors and unitary councils of approximately 500,000 population. An implementation board of all current chief executives meets fortnightly to coordinate preparedness at proposal level.
findings.matters: Fundamental structural change to council operations and financial arrangements would materially affect a lender's assessment of creditworthiness, service continuity and covenant security. The depth of collaborative preparation suggests serious transition planning.
findings.figures: 1.5m population strategic authorities; 500,000 population unitary target; 11 councils collaborating; implementation board meeting fortnightly
findings.quote: The Government is expected to consider the various representations, with a decision being announced in June/July 2026.

findings.headline: Council has secured 3-year funding settlement with visibility of budget shortfalls in years 2 and 3 for medium-term planning
findings.detail: The announcement of a 3-year funding settlement provides unprecedented planning certainty. The council can now identify and plan to mitigate each year's budget shortfall in advance, rather than facing the one-year certainty that has historically limited medium-term planning.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council has sufficient planning horizon to manage emerging deficits proactively rather than facing sudden budget shocks. This represents a material change in financial planning capability.
findings.figures: Years 2 and 3 of 3-year settlement
findings.quote: Following the announcement of the 3-year funding settlement, the future funding shortfall is now clearer and is known sufficiently in advance for strategic planning to mitigate each annual shortfall in years 2 and 3.

findings.headline: Three corporate risks de-escalated to service-level management since March 2026
findings.detail: Three risks have been moved from the corporate risk register to service-level management: Quality of Planning Committee Decisions (CR8), Corporate Property Fire Safety (CR15), and Emergency Recovery (CR17). This signals risk improvements or greater confidence in service-level mitigation in these areas.
findings.matters: De-escalation of risks indicates improvement in specific risk areas and that prior corporate-level attention is no longer needed.
findings.figures: Three risks de-escalated
findings.quote: CR8 Quality of Planning Committee Decisions: This risk has been de-escalated from the CRR and will be managed at a service level.

findings.headline: Cost of Living Crisis impact rated 16, matching target 16, indicating sustained external pressure expected
findings.detail: The council rates the risk and impact of the Cost of Living Crisis on its residents and service demand at 16, with the target also set at 16, meaning the council expects this pressure to persist and aims to manage rather than reduce it.
findings.matters: Sustained cost of living pressure suggests long-term elevated demand for council services and ongoing revenue and cost pressures that are not expected to ease.
findings.figures: CR11 rating 16, target 16
findings.quote: CR11 Cost of Living Crisis Head of Revenues, Benefits & Leisure 16  16

findings.headline: Housing rent error identified and being corrected, risk rating declining from 12 to target of 3
findings.detail: A housing rent error has been identified and is the subject of a correction process. The risk rating stands at 12 with a target of 3, indicating material correction activity is underway and expected to substantially reduce the risk.
findings.matters: Rent collection errors suggest control weaknesses or payment problems and the correction process itself carries financial implications for both council and tenants.
findings.figures: CR18 rating 12, target 3
findings.quote: CR18 Housing Rent Error Correction Head of Housing & Health 12  3

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation and devolution risk rated 20 against target of 15
findings.detail: The Chief Executive has rated devolution and potential local government reorganisation as a corporate risk at 20, tied as the highest risk rating. The council aims to reduce this to 15. This reflects material structural uncertainty potentially facing the council.
findings.matters: Structural reorganisation of local government can have significant implications for council finances, operations, and service delivery; a lender needs visibility of this scenario risk.
findings.figures: CR19 rating 20, target 15
findings.quote: CR19 Devolution and Local Government Reorganisation Chief Executive 20  15

findings.headline: Financial Sustainability risk rated 20 against target of 12
findings.detail: The council has identified Financial Sustainability as a significant corporate risk with a current rating of 20, the highest severity band, and a target rating of 12. This is the shared highest risk rating in the corporate register alongside Local Government Reorganisation.
findings.matters: A lender and council finance director need to understand what is driving this significant financial sustainability concern and what the council's plan is to address the gap from 20 to target of 12.
findings.figures: CR7 rating 20, target 12
findings.quote: CR7 Financial Sustainability Head of Finance, Property & Climate Resilience 20  12

findings.headline: Staffing savings identified by managers proposed to be counted at only 20-40% due to dependence on natural turnover which cannot be guaranteed
findings.detail: Multiple service budget options contain proposals for staffing reductions. Officers state these are "only possible through natural staff turnover and therefore cannot be guaranteed." Furthermore, "these savings will further stretch service delivery and is likely to lead to lower levels of service provision if agreed." As a result, only 20% (£43k) or 40% (£87k) of total stated staffing savings is being assumed in the budget, through an increase to the existing £282k Vacancy Target.
findings.matters: Staffing savings dependent on turnover are inherently uncertain. Relying on only partial counting of these savings leaves hidden budget risk—if turnover does not materialise at assumed rates, the council will face unplanned overspends.
findings.figures: £282k existing Vacancy Target; £43k (20% of staffing savings) or £87k (40% of staffing savings) proposed increase
findings.quote: This will only be possible through natural staff turnover and therefore cannot be guaranteed. Furthermore, these savings will further stretch service delivery and is likely to lead to lower levels of service provision if agreed. Therefore, it is proposed that only a proportion of the overall value is assumed within the budget, increasing the existing £282k Vacancy Target within the baseline by either £43k (20% of total saving, amber risk) or £87k (40% of total saving, red risk).

findings.headline: Mid Devon Housing reviewing viability and sustainability of ambitious housing development programme against HRA affordability
findings.detail: The HRA's deficits are partly driven by "the rising cost of financing the ambitious housing development programme." Mid Devon Housing is currently reviewing the development programme's viability, specifically testing: the balance between new build ambition versus HRA sustainability; tenure mix (social versus affordable); build specification (net zero versus EPC B); cost assumptions and borrowing requirements; and grant funding availability. This review signals concern about whether the development programme as currently scoped is affordable within the HRA.
findings.matters: A large council housing development programme under viability review suggests the council may need to scale back, delay, or restructure the programme, which would materially affect capital spend and HRA financing costs.
findings.figures: HRA shortfall driven by rising development programme financing costs; specific cost figures for alternative programme options not yet available
findings.quote: Currently Mid Devon Housing is reviewing their viability and sustainability, particularly in respect of the ambitious development programme. Specifically, the review will be considering: Balancing new build ambition vs HRA sustainability

findings.headline: General Fund shortfall forecast to expand from £1.601m in 2027/28 to £5.486m by 2029/30; HRA from £1.491m to £5.923m
findings.detail: The General Fund shortfall grows from £1,601k in 2027/28 to £5,486k by 2029/30. The HRA shortfall grows from £1,491k to £5,923k over the same period. Both are driven by reduction in funding from the Local Government Finance Settlement, inflation assumptions, and service pressures that are not offset by identified savings. This expansion signals structural deficits rather than cyclical pressures.
findings.matters: While 2027/28 may be balanced through reserve drawdowns, the out-year position shows deficits that will require either material service changes or further reserve depletion if they materialise, signalling medium-term sustainability concerns.
findings.quote: For the General Fund, this estimated a funding shortfall for 2027/28 of £1,601k, and is due to rise significantly to £5,486k by 2029/30. This forecast is largely driven by the reduction in funding as announced within the Local Government Finance Settlement and assumptions for inflation and known service pressures.

findings.headline: HRA 2027/28 shortfall of £884k proposed to be met through £442k of savings not yet identified and £442k draw from reserves
findings.detail: The HRA faces a 2027/28 shortfall of £884k after adjustments. Officers have not yet identified specific pressures or savings options. The report proposes this shortfall be managed through £442k of unidentified savings and £442k drawn from reserves. The paper acknowledges that "given the scale of the likely shortfall, it is unlikely that a sufficient level can be identified to fully balance the 2027/28 budget without significant implications on service provision or draw from reserves."
findings.matters: The HRA budget is not actually balanced—half the required savings remain to be found. This leaves material uncertainty about whether the council can deliver its 2027/28 budget without further service restrictions or borrowing.
findings.figures: £884k forecast shortfall, £442k possible savings (not identified), £442k reserve draw
findings.quote: Currently the review of the HRA continues and therefore, at this time, there have not been any specific HRA budget pressures or savings identified by officers. Therefore, there are no proposals directly to be considered, and these will follow in future Cabinet reports.

findings.headline: Mid Devon's £1,601k General Fund shortfall for 2027/28 to be managed through reducing reserve contributions by £642k and drawing £500k from reserves
findings.detail: The General Fund faces a shortfall of £1,601k in 2027/28 before addressing it with budget options. After identifying Green and Amber budget pressures and savings options and a business rates forecast update, the revised shortfall stands at £1,142k. The council proposes to close this gap by reducing planned contributions to reserves by £642k and drawing £500k from reserves (from £2,091k General Fund plus £17,327k Earmarked Reserves), leaving circa £19m in reserves.
findings.matters: A finance director needs to know whether deficits are being closed through service changes or one-off reserve movements, as the latter masks structural pressures and cannot be repeated indefinitely.
findings.figures: £1,601k initial shortfall, £1,142k revised shortfall, £642k reduced reserve contributions, £500k reserve draw, £2,091k General Fund Reserve held, £17,327k Earmarked Reserves held
findings.quote: Similarly, the review of reserves indicates that funding could be drawn from reserves without reducing our resilience. As at 31 March 2026, the Council holds £2,091k in the General Fund Reserve, £91k above the recommended minimum, plus £17,327k in Earmarked Reserves held for various reasons. Combined, a similar value of £500k could be drawn from reserves, to help mitigate the forecast shortfall, leaving circa £19m in reserves if required.

Year 2 shows £106k ongoing costs.
findings.matters: Substantial unplanned capital and systems investment needs indicate ageing IT infrastructure and emerging compliance/security requirements now pressing, material for lenders assessing capital demands on council finances.

The paper states these are either not immediately realisable or would not be recommended due to severe negative impact on service delivery, reflecting administration priority to protect service delivery and avoid redundancies.
findings.matters: Explicit constraint on available savings options shows limited financial flexibility and governance priority for service protection over fiscal recovery, material for peer finance directors and lenders assessing recovery capacity.

findings.detail: The pressures section records a £100k allocation for climate change as a high-risk item for 2027/28-2028/29, indicating emerging spending demands from strategic priorities that will require future budget solutions.
findings.matters: It signals the council has identified new spending commitments beyond the current budget cycle that will need funding; combined with income-dependent savings proposals, this indicates structural budget pressure.

findings.detail: The document explicitly marks the £20k PPA income increase as temporary because MHCLG has indicated it may pursue full or 90% Development Management cost recovery fee setting. The note states this would negate the need for the one-off additional PPA resource in the medium term.
findings.matters: The sustainability of this savings stream depends on government policy decisions not yet made; if MHCLG introduces cost-recovery powers, the council's PPA strategy becomes obsolete and the savings option disappears.

findings.detail: Planning Performance Agreement income is proposed to increase from £20k to £40k (marked as one-off), and Fees & Charges are proposed to increase by £50k, together representing approximately £70k of the £73.5k total savings identified. The document notes that PPA income increases should reflect the service acquiring additional consultant capacity to handle demand.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders track whether councils fund budget solutions through sustainable cost reductions or volatile income sources; planning income depends on housing market activity and speculative applications, which fluctuate.

This totals against only £20,000 in new pressures for the same period. The volume and risk profile of options suggests significant budget pressure.
findings.matters: The volume and risk weighting of savings options indicates the intensity of budget pressure facing the council and suggests limited room for low-risk measures.
findings.figures: Total savings options 2027/28: £395,000 (low risk £70k, medium/high risk £325k); total pressures £20,000
findings.quote: Green and Amber Savings (395.000)

findings.headline: Creative communities grants and business support programs considered for removal despite being flagged as effective and politically important

Business support contribution (£10k) faces removal despite members being 'very keen to support this', with the paper noting removal 'would be reputationally damaging should we be the only authority not to support our local businesses in this manner.'
findings.matters: This signals budget pressure severe enough to force cuts to programmes the council identifies as working and politically important. It indicates constraints on the council's capacity to deliver stated priorities.
findings.figures: Creative communities grants £30k; business support £10k
findings.quote: The scheme has been popular with members and our local communities. It has been one of the few opportunities we have as a council to increase footfall in our town centres. Potentially these grants could be removed from the budget for 2027/28.

findings.headline: Maintenance spending reductions totalling £275,000 explicitly flagged as carrying insurance claim risks
findings.detail: The council plans cuts to leisure centre maintenance (£100k), general maintenance (£100k), Market Walk upkeep (£50k), and waste depot maintenance (£25k). Multiple items carry explicit risk language: 'Risks are reputational, possible additional insurance claims against the council'. This disclosure suggests the council recognises that cost-cutting in maintenance areas could create legal or insurance exposure.
findings.matters: Lenders assess whether councils are managing their asset base properly. Insurance claims from deferred maintenance would hit reserves. Explicit risk disclosure suggests awareness of this exposure.
findings.figures: Leisure centre maintenance £100k; general maintenance £100k; Market Walk £50k; waste depot £25k
findings.quote: Risks are reputational, possible additional insurance claims against the council but better maintained than ever

findings.paper_title: SD&CI PDG - Appendix 4 Budget Options Oct Cabinet
findings.headline: Service demand growth is driving permanent staffing commitments and capacity increases across waste and recycling
findings.detail: The council is converting two temporary waste management roles to permanent positions (£53k and £14k), adding an extra recycling collection round (£185k), and increasing residual waste capacity (£152k). These are driven by "existing round pressures and an increase in residents", signalling that housing growth is creating structural demand that requires permanent cost increases, not one-off solutions.
findings.matters: Once staffing is made permanent, the cost is locked in; if housing growth is driving service demand, these costs will likely continue to rise, reducing flexibility to respond to future pressures

findings.paper_title: Mid Devon DC Auditor's Annual Report 2025-26 Draft for Audit Committee
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account deficit of £852k driven by voids from regulatory compliance works

findings.paper_title: Mid Devon DC Auditor's Annual Report 2025-26 Draft for Audit Committee
findings.headline: Unresolved social rent calculation liability remains outstanding with DWP
findings.detail: Historic issue: council failed to set tenant rents to formula requirements for many years. Made refund payments of £780k in 2025/26 to non-welfare tenants. Provision reduced from £1.8m (2024/25) to £921k (2025/26). Council remains in discussions with DWP over settlement for welfare-recipient tenants, leaving final liability uncertain.

findings.figures: £921k provision remaining; £780k refunds paid in 2025/26; prior provisions £1.8m (2024/25), £1.5m (2023/24)

findings.paper_title: Mid Devon DC Auditor's Annual Report 2025-26 Draft for Audit Committee
findings.headline: General Fund projected three-year deficit fell from £13.3m to £4.5m between September 2025 and February 2026 with no explanation
findings.detail: September 2025 MTFP identified cumulative deficits of £3.35m (2026/27), £4.7m (2027/28) and £5.79m (2028/29) totalling £13.3m. findings.matters: A two-thirds reduction in projected deficits signals either substantial unplanned savings or unrealistic budget assumptions. A lender must understand which.

findings.paper_title: Mid Devon District Council Audit Completion Report 2025-26 - Version to Audit Committee
findings.headline: Defined benefit pension gross surplus deteriorated by £1m while reported net liability improved marginally to £9.2m
findings.detail: The Council's gross defined benefit pension surplus on the LGPS decreased from £6.1m to £5.1m. However, under IFRIC 14 asset ceiling guidance the surplus is not recognised; instead a net pension liability of £9.2m is reported (2024/25: £9.6m), a £400k improvement. The discount rate used by the actuary increased from 5.80% to 6.10%. The reported improvement masks deterioration in the underlying funded position and is primarily driven by technical accounting adjustments.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities are material long-term financial obligations for councils; deterioration in the funded position indicates increased future contribution requirements, though the quantum of reported liability has marginally improved.
findings.figures: £6.1m to £5.1m (gross deficit movement), £9.6m to £9.2m (reported net liability), 5.80% to 6.10% (discount rate), £9.2m net liability (6.7x materiality threshold)
findings.quote: a net liability recognised of £9.2m (2024/25: £9.6m)

findings.headline: Updating Business Rates forecast to local basis could reduce 2027/28 shortfall by £600k, subject to validation

The council estimates Business Rates growth of approximately £300k per year and proposes switching to a local forecast instead, potentially delivering £600k reduction in shortfall. findings.matters: One of the few controllable sources of relief from the budget gap, but dependent on assumption validation; if local growth is slower than estimated, this saving would not materialise and the shortfall would worsen.

findings.detail: The council proposes to revise its Business Rates forecast upward by approximately £600k by switching from settlement-based projections (based on 2024 baseline) to a local forecast incorporating two years of growth and inflation. Officers estimate circa £300k average growth in Business Rates annually.
findings.matters: The £600k adjustment is material to closing the budget gap; if the local forecast does not validate or growth does not materialise, the council would need to identify alternative savings or further erode reserves.
findings.figures: £600k, £300k (average annual growth)
findings.quote: This is based upon 2024 taxbase and multipliers, meaning there is the opportunity to recognise two years' worth of growth and inflation if the figure is switched to a local forecast. On average, there is circa £300k of growth in Business Rates each year, therefore, subject to validation of the local forecast, an estimated £600k reduction in the projected shortfall may be achievable.

findings.committee: Service Delivery & Continuous Improvement Policy Development Group
findings.paper_title: SD & CI PDG Report - MTFP Sept 2026
findings.headline: 2027/28 budget balanced through £500k one-off draw from reserves and £641k reduction in reserve contributions
findings.detail: The council proposes to close the 2027/28 shortfall using £500k drawn from existing reserves and £641k from reduced planned contributions to reserves. The General Fund Reserve stands at £2,091k as of 31 March 2026, only £91k above the recommended minimum of £2m.
findings.matters: Reliance on one-off reserve moves to balance the budget is unsustainable and signals limited headroom to absorb shocks, which concerns both finance directors and lenders assessing financial resilience.
findings.figures: £500k (reserve draw), £641k (reduced contributions), £2,091k (General Fund Reserve), £2m (minimum level)
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2026, the Council holds £2,091k in the General Fund Reserve, £91k above the recommended minimum, plus £17,327k in Earmarked Reserves held for various reasons. Combined, a similar value of £500k could be drawn from reserves, to help mitigate the forecast shortfall, leaving circa £19m in reserves if required.

findings.committee: Service Delivery & Continuous Improvement Policy Development Group
findings.headline: Council is modeling parking charge increases (5% and 10%) and garden waste charge increases (£1–£2 per year) to generate £50k–£171k in savings across scenarios
findings.detail: The paper shows the council testing multiple income-raising options. Parking tariffs at 5% (10p per hour) are modeled as medium risk; at 10% (20p per hour) as high risk. Garden waste can be grown through £1/year increases (medium risk) or £2/year (high risk, due to customer loss risk). Trade waste fees offer additional upside. These are demand-sensitive options with explicit acknowledged downsides.
findings.matters: A finance director or peer council needs to know whether the deficit strategy rests on volume growth (marketing, new residents) or price increases that carry customer churn risk
findings.figures: Parking 5% increase (medium risk); parking 10% increase (high risk); garden waste current subscriptions 11,776; garden waste £1 increase medium risk, £2 increase high risk
findings.quote: Projection on Parking Income from customers by increasing fees (Budget for 2026-27 £894k). An increase in tariffs would bring in potential additional income but there would be the risk of drop off in usage Forecast to meet budget (low risk). To increase tariffs by 5% (10p on 1 hour) is medium risk To increase tariffs by 10% (20p for 1 hour) is high risk respectively.

Both have been in place for 14 months and are now confirmed as ongoing. This is a structural staff cost increase.

findings.headline: Waste service expansion costs £337k cumulatively: extra recycling round (£185k) and residual waste capacity (£152k)
findings.detail: Population growth and existing service pressures are forcing the council to add operating capacity: one extra recycling round and increased residual waste round capacity. Both are modeled as pressures. The council says the recycling round is driven by existing pressures and new housing; the residual waste increase is to reduce round sizes and accommodate new housing.
findings.matters: A council facing similar housing growth needs to understand the service cost implications; a lender assessing the council's financial resilience needs to know whether growth is funding growth or creating a subsidy

findings.quote: Increase in recycling capacity due to needing to put on an extra recycling round to deal with existing round pressures and an increase in residents.

findings.headline: Former tenancy refunds underway: 50 completed by July 2026; 57 targeted by September 2026; 316 pending data validation; 200 UC-related pending
findings.detail: Of 623 former tenancy cases identified, 107 non-benefit cases prioritised: 50 fully processed by end July 2026 with 57 remaining targeted for completion by end September 2026. A further 316 HB-related cases require data validation due for completion October 2026, after which tenant and DWP refunds can be processed. Remaining 200 former tenancies with UC element must await DWP national guidance.
findings.matters: Shows ongoing liability to former tenants with extended timeline into next financial year. Completion dependent on data validation completion and DWP resolution, creating further cash flow uncertainty for HRA.
findings.figures: 623 former cases identified; 107 non-benefit (50 completed, 57 pending); 316 HB cases pending validation; 200 UC cases pending
findings.quote: As of the end of July 2026, 50 of these cases have been fully processed with the remaining 57 cases due for completion by the end of September 2026.

findings.headline: Regulator of Social Housing engaged throughout; July 2026 meeting noted successful progress with no material concerns raised
findings.detail: Council self-referred to Regulator immediately upon identifying error. Regular engagement meetings held with RSH to provide assurance on action plan delivery and tenant redress. Council submits detailed evidence against RSH-prescribed requirements including committee reports, statistics, communications, DWP engagement updates, and action tracker. Most recent RSH meeting in July 2026 noted successful progress; no material concerns raised.
findings.matters: External validation of council's response approach reduces compliance and regulatory risk. Absence of concerns from regulator provides third-party assurance of sound approach despite ongoing UC blockage.
findings.figures: Regular RSH engagement; most recent July 2026; no material concerns raised
findings.quote: This evidence continues to be well received and fully meets the ongoing engagement requirements of the RSH . As noted in the previous update, we continue to meet with the RSH regularly, most recently in July 2026. Successful progress has been noted and no material concerns raised.

findings.headline: Total financial impact to HRA not disclosed; HRA balance may fall below agreed minimum level
findings.detail: Council decided not to recover undercharged amounts from tenants who were undercharged, placing full cost of overcharges on the HRA. While significant financial modelling has been undertaken, the paper does not disclose the total quantum. Risk assessment explicitly notes that HRA balance may drop below its agreed minimum level, reducing ability to withstand economic, legislative or climatic shocks. Potential need to reprioritise capital works including decarbonisation.
findings.matters: Shows direct impact on HRA viability and reserve adequacy. Lenders and peer councils need the total quantum to assess HRA headroom and debt capacity. Undisclosed quantum in a finance paper is a notable gap.
findings.figures: Minimum agreed HRA balance at risk; decarbonisation works reprioritisation possible if quantum is large
findings.quote: Allowing the HRA balance to drop below its minimum agreed balance for a period of time clearly reduces its ability to withstand any unknown economic/legislative/climatic shocks.

findings.headline: Historic evictions review completed; no possession cases identified where rent error was a material factor
findings.detail: Completed review of historic evictions involving rent arrears element. Initial caseload of 70 possession cases reduced to approximately 35 after removing cases with historic underpayment. Detailed manual cross-referencing of historic records confirmed that in all reviewed cases, the historic rent overcharge was not a material factor in the eviction decision.
findings.matters: Eliminates additional liability exposure from potential eviction-related claims by former tenants. Demonstrates thorough risk mitigation approach using documented methodology.
findings.figures: 70 initial possession cases reviewed; approximately 35 required detailed review; zero cases where rent error was material factor
findings.quote: Work has now been completed on the review of a small number of historic evictions (possession cases) on former tenancies with a rent debt element with no evictions identified where the historic rent error was a material factor.

findings.headline: Universal Credit refund issue escalated to Treasury level; approximately 20 councils nationally flagged similar rent issues to DWP
findings.detail: DWP remains unable to share Universal Credit claimant information due to its own rules, preventing the council from apportioning refunds between tenants and the DWP. DWP has not confirmed how it will calculate overpayments or agree a repayment process. Multiple escalations by the Deputy Chief Executive (S151) have produced no progress. The issue has been raised to Treasury level due to complexity affecting approximately 20 councils nationally.
findings.matters: Identifies a systemic national barrier affecting multiple councils simultaneously. Peer councils would need to monitor this closely given its impact on HRA planning, cash flow certainty, and reserve adequacy.
findings.figures: Approximately 20 councils flagged similar rent issues to DWP nationally
findings.quote: This is a national issue and t he DWP have confirmed that matters around information sharing, and incorrect rents continue to be raised at "Treasury" level due to the complexity of the problem and circa 20 Councils are flagging similar rent issues with them.

findings.headline: Current tenancies: 547 cases (46%) resolved with £301k tenant refunds and £464k DWP subsidy refund; 639 cases (54%) pending DWP Universal Credit guidance
findings.detail: Of 1,186 current tenancy cases identified, 547 have been fully processed: 225 non-benefit and 322 Housing Benefit cases with £301k refunded directly to tenants (99% claimed by end July 2026) plus £464k refunded to DWP for Housing Benefit overpayments. However, 639 current tenants (54%) with Universal Credit involvement remain unresolved pending national DWP guidance on information sharing and overpayment calculation.
findings.matters: Shows material progress but significant unresolved exposure. The UC block creates cash flow uncertainty, ongoing HRA liability, and unpredictable timeline for completing this cohort.
findings.figures: 1,186 current cases identified; 547 (46%) processed; 639 (54%) pending; £301k refunded to tenants; £464k refunded to DWP
findings.quote: The remaining circa 54% relates to cases with an element of UC involvement and is around 639 current tenants of the 1186 current tenants overall that have been historically overcharged.

findings.headline: Historic rent calculation error identified during audit; baseline recalculated and independently verified January 2025
findings.detail: Error resulted from incorrect application of the government's rent calculation formula (introduced 2001) affecting all tenants' charges over multiple years. The error involved incorrectly averaged property valuations. Baseline was recalculated and independently verified in January 2025, with all rents correct from that date forward.
findings.matters: Demonstrates an audit control gap (error undetected for years under previous auditors). Peer councils would need to verify their own rent-setting controls, particularly around staff resource and audit continuity.
findings.figures: Rent formula formula introduced 2001; error in application identified and corrected January 2025
findings.quote: This baseline re-calculation was completed in January 2025 and independently verified. All rents have therefore been correct since this date.

findings.detail: The HRA's share of corporate and democratic costs is budgeted at £215,440 for 2026/27, up £37,850 from £177,590 in 2025/26. This represents a 21% increase in the allocation of overhead costs to the HRA.
findings.matters: A 21% year-on-year increase in allocated corporate costs is a material pressure on HRA finances; finance directors track overhead allocations as cost drivers affecting HRA affordability.
